topic: SC: internet access is a fundamental right of every person, including children - no blanket social media bans for kids; stronger steps against online child abuse material (Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish, 2026 INSC 1149, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1063)

slides.title: Internet access is your **fundamental right**
slides.subtitle: The Supreme Court says this right belongs to **every person**, and children have it too.
slides.cite: **Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish**, 2026 INSC 1149 · Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran

slides.label: What the court held
slides.title: A right under **Articles 21 and 19(1)(a)**
bullets: Accessing and using the internet is a **fundamental right**, linked to the right to life and the freedom of speech.
Free speech includes the right to **receive and share information**. For many children in remote areas, the internet is their main way to learn.
Children hold this right **whatever their age**.

slides.label: No blanket ban
slides.title: Do not punish the **victim**
bullets: The court accepted that the internet is not safe for children today, but said cutting them off treats the **victim as the problem**.
It called blanket social media bans for kids **unproven** and disproportionate. Children may simply move to less safe platforms.
Age checks could also mean constant collection of **sensitive data**.
slides.note: **Safety and freedom are not opposites.** The court said children are entitled to both.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: This is **not** a free-for-all
bullets: Age-based safeguards are still allowed: **parental consent** and oversight, a "child mode", private accounts by default, and limits on contact from strangers.
The government can still block content that is **harmful in itself**, such as adult websites.

slides.label: Fighting online abuse
slides.title: Tougher rules for **platforms**
bullets: The court set out steps to detect and remove child sexual abuse material, including a **national database** so content removed by one platform is flagged on others.
Reports must be easy to file, can be **anonymous**, and must be acknowledged within **24 hours**. The Centre reports back on **10 December 2026**.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Is using the internet a fundamental right? The Supreme Court says yes, and children have it too 🌐⚖️

The Supreme Court has held that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right under Article 21 (right to life) read with Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech, which includes receiving and sharing information). The court noted that for many children, especially in remote areas, the internet is often their only source of learning.

The court refused to back a blanket social media ban for children. It said keeping kids off the internet treats the victim as the problem, may push them to less safe platforms, and age checks could mean constant collection of sensitive data. But safeguards are still allowed: parental consent and oversight, a "child mode", private accounts by default and limits on contact from strangers. The government can still block content that is harmful in itself, like adult websites.

The court also set out stronger steps against online child sexual abuse material, including a national database so that content removed by one platform is flagged on others, easy and anonymous reporting, and acknowledgement of complaints within 24 hours. The Centre has to report its progress on 10 December 2026.

Case: Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish, 2026 INSC 1149, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1063
Bench: Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, Supreme Court of India
